subject: Banking
title: Net Interest Margin Explained
description: A quick win: understand Net Interest Margin Explained.

hook.text: Banks pay you 0.5% on your savings. They charge borrowers 7%. That 6.5% gap is where the profit lives.

buildup.text: The net interest margin is the difference between what a bank earns on loans and what it pays on deposits.

discovery.text: A typical bank makes 2-3% NIM. On $100 billion in assets, that's $2-3 billion in annual revenue from the spread alone.

twist.text: When interest rates drop near zero, the spread shrinks.

climax.text: The interest spread is banking's oldest trick. Borrow cheap, lend expensive, keep the difference.

punchline.text: Pay low, charge high. The interest spread is banking's core engine.

quiz.question: What is net interest margin?
options: The gap between loan income and deposit costs

details.summary: Net interest margin is the fundamental metric of bank profitability, measuring the difference between what a bank earns on loans and investments versus what it pays depositors. The typical US bank NIM hovers around 3 percent.
details.whyItMatters: NIM is the core engine of banking profit. Every banking product, strategy, and risk decision ultimately aims to protect or expand this margin, making it the single most important number in understanding bank economics.
takeaways: NIM equals interest earned minus interest paid divided by average earning assets
US bank NIM typically ranges from 2.5 to 3.5 percent
Low interest rate environments compress NIM and hurt bank profitability

faq.question: How does a bank improve its net interest margin?
faq.answer: Banks can improve NIM by raising loan rates, lowering deposit costs, shifting to higher-yielding asset classes, or extending loan durations. In practice, competition limits how much banks can adjust either side unilaterally.

faq.question: Why does NIM matter more than total revenue?
faq.answer: NIM measures profitability per dollar of assets, showing how efficiently a bank converts its balance sheet into income. A bank with massive assets but thin NIM may earn less than a smaller bank with better spread management.
